Existing solutions to mitigate test-time inference costs, such as retraining with fewer training images or compressing models through pruning or quantization, are inadequate for industrial environments. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to reduce inference costs using a trainable layer that generates binary feature representations from a compressed object detection model during test-time. Our method leverages a unique combination of entropy and feature similarity measures to optimize the compression ratio and ensure the preserved information is most relevant. Experimental results on the MS-COCO dataset show that our approach achieves a 2.7x speedup with only 10% accuracy loss when compressing object detection models, outperforming the best compression techniques in terms of speedup-to-compression ratio. Moreover, our method allows for dynamic compression during test-time based on the number of objects in an image, achieving a balance between speedup and accuracy. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel method called Self-Supervised Occlusion-Aware NeRF (SO-NeRF) that enables scene understanding and separation of objects at different depths without relying on explicit depth cues. Our approach uses an encoder-decoder architecture that leverages self-supervised learning to minimize the difference between the rendered and original images, then uses a feature matching loss to achieve depth-consistent feature representations. Our method can be trained end-to-end and achieves competitive results in both NeRF reconstruction and 3D scene interpretation. We discovered that adversarial attacks can cause significant changes to the internal representations of DNNs, leading to a loss of useful information. As a result, when the model tries to learn from these altered inputs, it becomes stuck in a non-convergent learning pattern. Our research provides a deeper understanding of the mechanisms behind these attacks and offers a new approach to mitigating the issue by incorporating additional features into the model. This research not only highlights the need for improved defenses against adversarial attacks but also underscores the importance of considering the impact of these attacks on internal representations when developing DNNs for automatic speech recognition. To our knowledge, this study is the first to examine the effects of adversarial attacks on end-to-end DNNs for automatic speech recognition. A promising solution to speed up RNN training is to divide the networks into smaller parts called tensor cores, and perform training computations within these cores. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of using tensor core-accelerated RNNs, and propose a new method called CoreAlign. This technique allows us to combine the computational and memory capabilities of tensor cores in a way that minimizes the impact of data dependencies between adjacent cores. By applying CoreAlign, we can significantly reduce the idle time of tensor cores, and make the most efficient use of their capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments on real-world NLP tasks, and show that CoreAlign can accelerate RNN training by 2.6-4.6 times compared to traditional methods, and outperforms other acceleration techniques by a large margin.
